rationale: B wins because it trims the fat and makes the missing facts part of the story instead of pretending around them. Its "Monzo's first profitable year, by the numbers — and what it isn't telling us yet" turns undisclosed CAC and US targets into an editorial pressure point; A's weaker "What Monzo's US Checking Account Actually Is — and What It Isn't" needs facts about restrictions it does not have. A has good bones, but B is the set a founder can take into reporter selection without first killing a padded consumer angle.
gaps_in_A: "what the partner-bank structure means it cannot deliver" asks the angle to claim product limits that are not in the update; the set only admits later it needs proof of lending, deposit limits, or transfers.

"Monzo's Partner-Bank Deal: What the Regulatory Structure Enables — and Where It Stops" is too close to "Monzo Returns to the US, This Time Without Chasing a Banking License" unless the partner bank/regulatory constraints are known.
"The prevailing narrative has been that neobanks sacrifice profitability indefinitely for growth" is plausible, but not supplied; it needs external evidence before becoming the spine of an angle.
"what the budgeting tools do that standard bank apps do not" exposes that the consumer angle has no differentiation in the brief.
gaps_in_B: "challenger banks burn cash, struggle to make money at scale, and have repeatedly failed to crack the US" is a broad category claim not in the update; source it or narrow it to Monzo.
"Both data points landed in the same reporting window" overstates the timing; the update says the profit was reported "this year," not necessarily alongside the launch.
"what the partner-bank model gives up (economics, control, branding)" names tradeoffs that may be true, but they are not facts in the brief yet. Keep them as questions until proved.
